content.text: No machine or device is perfect. When energy is transferred from one store to another, some energy is always dissipated (spread out) in forms that are not useful — usually as thermal energy due to friction, electrical resistance, or air resistance.
is the measure of how well a device converts input energy into useful output energy.

Understanding efficiency is crucial for engineering, environmental science, and everyday life. More efficient devices waste less energy, cost less to run, and have a smaller environmental impact. In this lesson, we will define efficiency, learn how to calculate it, explore Sankey diagrams, and examine ways to improve the efficiency of machines and devices.
is the ratio of useful energy output to total energy input, often expressed as a percentage.
\text{total energy input} = \text{useful energy output} + \text{wasted energy output}

An efficiency of 100% would mean all input energy is converted to useful output — this is theoretically impossible for most machines due to friction and other losses.
Efficiency cannot be greater than 100%, as that would violate conservation of energy.

Converts kinetic energy to thermal energy. Surfaces become warm.
Opposes motion and transfers kinetic energy to thermal energy in the air.
When current flows through wires and components, some electrical energy is transferred to thermal energy.
Vibrating components produce sound waves, transferring energy to the surroundings.
Some devices produce light when it is not the intended output (e.g., an electric motor may glow slightly).

Dissipated energy has not been destroyed — it still exists — but it has been spread out into the surroundings and is no longer in a concentrated, useful form. It is practically impossible to collect this energy and use it again.

| Device | Typical Efficiency | Main Energy Waste |
|---|---|---|
| Electric heater | ~100% (for heating purposes) | Virtually none (all electrical energy becomes thermal) |
| Electric motor | 80-95% | Thermal (friction, resistance), sound |
| Petrol car engine | 25-30% | Thermal (exhaust gases, cooling) |
| Diesel engine | 30-40% | Thermal |
| Coal power station | 30-40% | Thermal (cooling water, exhaust) |
| Gas power station (combined cycle) | 50-60% | Thermal |
| Solar panel | 15-25% | Reflected/transmitted light, thermal |
| LED light bulb | 25-35% | Thermal |
| Incandescent light bulb | 3-5% | Thermal |
| Human body (mechanical work) | ~25% | Thermal |
Note: An electric heater is nearly 100% efficient
, because thermal energy is the desired output. However, it may not be the most efficient way to heat a room compared to a heat pump.
There are many ways to improve the efficiency of machines and devices:
Using lubricants (oil, grease) between moving parts.
Using ball bearings or roller bearings.
Streamlining the shape of vehicles and machines.
Operating in lower-density environments where possible.
Using materials with lower resistivity (e.g., copper instead of steel).
Using superconductors at very low temperatures (zero resistance).
Insulating hot surfaces to reduce thermal energy losses to the surroundings.
Insulating buildings to reduce heating/cooling losses.
Using more efficient components (e.g., LEDs instead of incandescent bulbs).
Recovering waste energy (e.g., regenerative braking in electric cars converts kinetic energy back to electrical energy).
Combined heat and power (CHP) systems use waste heat from electricity generation for space heating.

Overall efficiency = efficiency of station × efficiency of motor:
This demonstrates that when multiple devices are connected in series, the overall efficiency is the product of the individual efficiencies.

A coal-fired power station receives 1000 MJ of chemical energy from coal. The useful electrical energy output is 350 MJ. Energy lost in the cooling tower is 500 MJ, and energy lost in the chimney (exhaust gases) is 100 MJ. (a) Calculate the efficiency. (b) Calculate any remaining energy loss. (c) Describe what a Sankey diagram for this would look like.
The Sankey diagram would have an input arrow of width proportional to 1000 MJ entering from the left. This splits into:
A 350 MJ arrow continuing to the right (useful electrical output)
A 500 MJ arrow branching downward (cooling tower losses)
A 100 MJ arrow branching downward (chimney losses)
A 50 MJ arrow branching downward (other losses)
The cooling tower arrow would be the widest of the waste arrows.
An old boiler has an efficiency of 65% and a new boiler has an efficiency of 92%. Both need to provide 10 kJ of useful thermal energy. Calculate the total energy input required for each.
The new boiler uses 29% less energy input, saving money and reducing carbon emissions.

In practice, no machine can achieve 100% efficiency. There are always some energy losses due to friction, resistance, or other factors. The second law of thermodynamics places fundamental limits on the efficiency of heat engines.
"An electric heater is inefficient because it produces heat instead of something useful."
If the purpose of the heater is to produce heat, then it is nearly 100% efficient — almost all the electrical energy is converted to thermal energy, which is the desired output.
Energy is never destroyed. Wasted energy is dissipated to the surroundings (usually as thermal energy), where it is spread out and cannot easily be used again.
This would violate conservation of energy. If a calculation gives an efficiency above 100%, there is an error.
"More efficient devices always cost less to buy."
Efficient devices sometimes cost more to buy but save money over time through lower running costs. The decision depends on the balance between purchase cost and energy savings.
"You can calculate efficiency by dividing output force by input force."
This gives mechanical advantage, not efficiency. Efficiency compares useful energy (or work) output to total energy (or work) input.
"The efficiency of a device is fixed."
Efficiency can change with operating conditions. For example, a car engine is more efficient at certain speeds and loads than others. Wear and tear can also reduce efficiency over time.
